extracted.intended_audience: photographers, photo editors, journalism readers and media-ethics observers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and apply standards for permissible image manipulation in news vs. magazine fashion/editorial contexts, and consider disclosure and credibility implications. Focuses on the New York Times' distinction between news photography and its T fashion magazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-photography manipulation limit
rubrics_metrics.description: 'minor color-toning and brightness for production purposes' only in news stories
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York Times editors strictly forbid any image manipulation beyond 'minor color-toning and brightness for production purposes' in news stories — the intent is to preserve the credibility and factual nature of news images. In practice this limits adjustments to production-level color/brightness corrections and excludes retouching that alters subject appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style-magazine (T) retouching allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Retouches and removal of blemishes are allowed in the style magazine's fashion photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: T magazine — though an editorial product produced by journalists — is treated differently: editors argue readers accept fashion photography as fantasy and thus tolerate retouching such as blemish removal or more extensive alterations (the article cites an editor saying she 'considered adding some fat to her with Photoshop'). This allowance recognizes different genre expectations but raises debates about consistency with newsroom standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / disclosure for retouched editorial images
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare when fashion/editorial images have been retouched so readers understand they present an ideal rather than reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A suggested best practice (mentioned in the discussion) is a prominent disclaimer: 'Many, perhaps all, of the photographic images in this fashion magazine have been retouched, sometimes lightly, sometimes with a heavier hand, sometimes in ways that would not be permissible in the New York Times newspaper. A fashion magazine presents an ideal, not reality.' Such disclosure is proposed to mitigate credibility risk when a news-branded organization publishes retouched imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-expectation distinction between news and fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers bring different expectations to news photography (realism, minimal alteration) versus fashion photography (fantasy, stylistic alteration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors argue that because fashion photography is about fantasy, readers do not expect the same fidelity as news images. However, critics note that when a fashion product is produced under a news organization's brand, that brand's reputation for factual accuracy complicates the permissibility of retouching and may risk the organization's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical concerns about body image and health implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of very thin models and heavy retouching may promote unhealthy body images and attract public complaint; some jurisdictions have model-BMI-related rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public complaints cited include claims that publishing extremely thin or heavily retouched models promotes an unhealthy body image. Commenters referenced that some countries restrict runway models below certain BMI thresholds. Editors and publishers should weigh social-health impacts and public reaction when permitting retouching or selecting models.
